title: Buying a Panhard Dyna Z12 from an advert: the file to obtain before travelling
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: Documents, serial number, underside photographs, cold start, missing parts and transport: requests that prevent a long journey based on a vague advert.
content:
A Dyna Z12 advert may consist of three photographs, an approximate year and the claim “engine turns”. That is enough to create interest, but not to justify a journey of several hundred miles. Before booking transport, build a small file: administrative identity, an ordered set of photographs, known history and an honest description of what genuinely works.

Clarify the identity being offered

Dyna Z covers several types and construction phases. Club Panhard dates Z12 production from August 1956 to October 1958. Ask for clear photographs of the manufacturer’s plate, serial number and registration, with personal details concealed if the seller prefers. Type, seat count, date and registered keeper should be capable of comparison.

Registration date alone does not prove trim. Luxe Spécial, Grand Luxe and the Grand Standing option succeed or overlap one another during Z12 production. Two-tone paint, decorative sabots and whitewall tyres provide clues but are easily replaced. A cautious description and regular papers are more valuable than a prestigious trim asserted without evidence.

Twelve photographs to request

  1. complete front at car height;
  2. complete rear and lamp arrangement;
  3. both sides without filters or strong backlight;
  4. front and rear door openings with doors open;
  5. front and rear floors from inside;
  6. underside of sills and lifting areas;
  7. suspension mountings and areas close to crossmembers;
  8. empty boot, including spare-wheel space;
  9. complete engine compartment;
  10. close views of engine, carburettor and cooling shrouds;
  11. dashboard, upholstery and door cards;
  12. plates, numbers and any old invoices.

These images need to be recent. A picture from before a long lay-up says nothing about current brakes, tyres or damp. Refusal to show any underside view when the car is accessible is useful information in itself; a seller who shows an imperfect repair makes a serious discussion easier.

Body structure before paint shine

Z12 has an all-steel shell and weighs more than early light-alloy Dyna Z cars. Floors, sills, door pillars, suspension mountings and old welds deserve more attention than gloss. Ask whether the car can be lifted safely and where it is normally supported. Fresh black coating underneath may protect a sound repair or conceal overlapping metal.

The front doors, hinged on the centre pillar, provide a simple check. A video of opening and closing may show drop, unusual effort or uneven gaps. It cannot replace a physical inspection, but identifies areas that deserve close attention during the visit.

“Running”, “driving” and “ready to use”

These phrases describe different conditions. A running engine may start from a temporary fuel supply while the tank, charging system or cooling equipment remains unfinished. A driving car may move across a yard without braking straight. “Ready to use” needs dated facts: recent distance, work completed, tyres, brakes, insurance and documents.

For a stored car, a genuine cold-start video is more useful than footage of an already warm engine. The seller can show temperature by touch, the dashboard before starting, initial behaviour, idle and sounds during the first minutes. If no video is possible, value the car as a project with unknown mechanical condition instead of treating the omission as automatic dishonesty.

Identify the 851 cc unit beyond the word Aérodyne

Early Z12 used M5. For the 1958 model year, a turbine and enclosing panels organised cooling on M5 Aérodyne. Ask for views of the complete assembly, not only the top of the engine. Missing shrouds, carburettor origin, wiring changes and visible leaks all affect the recommissioning budget.

The 50 hp Tigre appeared in 1959, after Z12 production. If one is fitted, it is a later conversion that may be appealing but should be described accurately. Invoices for an exchange engine or rebuild often establish when and how the change occurred.

Price the missing pieces

A lamp, hubcap, moulding or upholstery fitting may seem minor beside a complete engine. On Grand Standing trim, a collection of scarce small parts can cost more than ordinary servicing. Make an inventory with club material and check actual availability before accepting that something is “easy to find”.

Club Panhard still supplies certain parts to members, but that does not mean every trim item is immediately available. A used component needing chrome, a piece requiring fabrication and a reproduction ready for fitting carry different prices and lead times.

Administrative questions before a deposit

FFVE advises buyers to secure proof of ownership and vehicle identity before a purchase intended for French historic registration. A car without registration is not automatically impossible to regularise, but it requires evidence of origin and the application can fail. Check the exact situation with official services before payment, based on the documents available and the intended registration.

Ask who is selling, where the car is kept, how long it has been owned and which documents will record the transfer. A deposit should follow written agreement on the vehicle, price, serial numbers, included parts and any clearly defined return conditions.

Make the visit a decision, not a discovery

On arrival, the car should confirm or contradict an organised file. Bring the photograph list, a light, clothing suitable for looking underneath and, if possible, someone familiar with Panhard. Record observed facts separately from the seller’s statements and work merely assumed.

Arrange transport before negotiating. A Dyna stored for years does not become a road-trip car because it starts. Trailer dimensions, access, free wheels, steering, handbrake, tie-down points and loose parts all belong to the purchase. A low price soon loses its attraction if removal has to be improvised.
